4.0.s.en: (2) The call to mankind to the life of the Lord

4.0.0.en: 2- O ye sons of men, how long will ye turn my glory into shame? how long will ye love vanity, and seek after leasing? Selah.

4.0.1.en: 1- David calls, with compassion, all mankind, first of them Saul, then Absalom, that they may not persist in their evils, turning his glory, because he is a king anointed by God, into shame by their pursuit of him, so that instead of being honored as a king he runs as a stranger everywhere, because he is threatened with death.

4.0.2.en: 2- By this he speaks about Christ also, whom, instead of honoring Him, the Jews crucified on the Cross of shame; they did not honor Him as the King of kings but crucified Him as a wicked criminal.

4.0.3.en: 3- David does not mean by this his own comfort, because he accepts everything from God, but he has compassion on sinners, the sons of men, for their separation from God and their wronging of His anointed, that is, David.

4.0.4.en: 4- The cause of the evil of the sons of men is their love of lusts and pride and all the vain material things in the world. All of them are false and will pass away, but they will be called to account for their sins, so he calls them to repentance and not to persist in evil.

4.0.5.en: 5- This verse ends with the word Selah, which is a musical pause, so that man may review himself and repent of his sins.

4.0.6.en: 6- He calls them sons of men so that they may reason as human beings and not be immersed in lusts like the animals, but he desires that they rise to spiritual thinking, care for the salvation of their souls, and live with God, so that they become like the saints, like angels on earth.

4.1.0.en: 3- But know that the Lord hath set apart him that is godly for himself: the Lord will hear when I call unto him.

4.1.1.en: 1- David alerts all mankind to an important truth, which is that God not only cares for David His godly one, or His chosen and holy one, as in the Septuagint, but also distinguishes him from the rest of mankind. This actually happened, for God rescued David from the hand of Saul, and gave him victory over him, since Saul fell into David's hand, and David pardoned him and did not harm him. In the end Saul died in the war, and David reigned in his place, and likewise God saved him from the hand of Absalom and gave him victory over him.

4.1.2.en: 2- David here is a type of Christ, who lived as a man among mankind, but God distinguished Him by the working of miracles and powerful teachings, and then He died and raised Himself.

4.1.3.en: 3- God always distinguishes His children and His people by His care for them and His work within them, so they enjoy God's presence with them on earth, as though they were in the Kingdom.

4.1.4.en: 4- The prophet David declares another truth in this verse, which is that the Lord answers him when he prays to Him; prayer is a means available to God's children to enter into God's presence, and He answers them, and so they feel reassured however much tribulations surround them, and indeed they enjoy meeting God at all times.

4.1.5.en: 5- David also declares to mankind that one of the most important means by which God shows His presence and power is His work in the one who fears Him and sanctifies his heart to Him. God declares Himself to those far from Him, either through creatures and the events of life, or through their seeing His work in His children, as David gave himself as an example in God's distinguishing him and answering his prayers, so that mankind may follow his example and believe in God and worship Him with all their hearts.

4.2.0.en: 4- Stand in awe, and sin not: commune with your own heart upon your bed, and be still. Selah.

4.2.1.en: 1- The prophet David calls mankind to tremble, that is, to fear God, so that they do not sin; it is a call to keep away from sin and to fortify oneself in the fear of God.

4.2.2.en: 2- In the Septuagint, that is, the Agpeya, it says "Be angry, and sin not", that is, let your anger be of the holy kind, in which there is no sin, as the Apostle Paul affirmed, quoting this same verse in (Eph 4:26). Holy anger is man's anger against his sins, his anger against evil and Satan, or his anger in the sense of firmness with those who err, until they repent.

4.2.3.en: 3- He also calls mankind, if they have sinned in their anger, to regret it and repent when they go into their chambers before they sleep on their beds. The idea of repentance every day before man sleeps is an idea that every person needs, and David experienced it when he made his bed to swim every night with his tears (Ps 6:6); that is, it is good that man be still and examine his thoughts and the intentions of his heart every night and repent of them before God.

4.2.4.en: 4- The verse ends with the word Selah, which is a musical pause for self-examination and repentance.

4.3.0.en: 5- Offer the sacrifices of righteousness, and put your trust in the Lord.

4.3.1.en: After David called mankind to keep away from sin, then to pray to God, who answers and distinguishes His children, and after that to repent every day, he adds here a positive work, which is offering the sacrifices of righteousness, and they are:

4.3.2.en: 1- Animal sacrifices on the altar of the Old Testament according to the Law of Moses, to offer repentance and love to God, all of which signify the sacrifice of Christ on the Cross, which we receive in the sacrament of the Eucharist, when we partake of the Body and Blood of the Lord, and so we are united with Him, and He works in us.

4.3.3.en: 2- The slaughter of the predatory animals and the beasts within us, that is, sins, through repentance, so the heart is purified.

4.3.4.en: 3- The slaughter of pride and self through humility.

4.3.5.en: 4- Offering ourselves as sacrifices poured out in the service of others, so we bear with them and forgive them and labor and give ourselves for their good.

4.3.6.en: 5- The sacrifice of emptying one's own will and relying on God and handing one's life over to Him, so we live reassured under His care.

4.3.7.en: 6- The sacrifice of praise, which is the prayers and thanksgiving and praise lifted up before God from hearts and lips.

4.3.8.en: God awaits from you sacrifices of love in prayer, worship and service, so do not be negligent in seizing every opportunity to draw near to God and serve Him.

4.4.0.en: 6- There be many that say, Who will shew us any good? Lord, lift thou up the light of thy countenance upon us.

4.4.1.en: 1- God's goodness extends to all mankind, but the prophet David wonders that some murmur and say, who will show us goodness, as though God had done no good with them. There is another meaning, which is that the men of God and the prophets, in the Old Testament, longed to see the good things, which appear in the person of Christ incarnate in the fullness of time.

4.4.2.en: 2- David answers the murmurers, who do not see God's goodness, and the righteous, who ask to see Christ, that God is able to lift up the light of His countenance upon His children, and in the Septuagint it says "The light of thy countenance, O Lord, hath shone upon us", and in the Greek translation "The light of thy countenance has been imprinted upon us", and this means that God shines and gives light upon His children with His light through the following:

4.4.3.en: a- The light by which man is distinguished from the rest of creatures through the spirit that is in him.

4.4.4.en: b- The light of faith in God and the enjoyment of His care and power.

4.4.5.en: c- The light of wisdom and discernment that He grants to His children, so they discern the good and reject evil and seek with love the depths of God.

4.4.6.en: d- The divine light and radiance, which is imprinted and pictured on the faces of God's children and shines upon others, so they see goodness through God's children who walk in righteousness.

4.4.7.en: 3- The face of Moses was clothed with intense brightness when he met God, and so also God's children in every generation, God gives them grace and awe in the eyes of those around them.

4.5.0.en: 7- Thou hast put gladness in my heart, more than in the time that their corn and their wine increased.

4.5.1.en: 1- As a result of God's shining upon David's heart, he felt gladness and joy greater than any gladness man receives on earth; human beings feel gladness because of their possessions, such as wine and wheat, especially when they are abundant, but all the material things of the world pass away, so man is exposed to fluctuation between joy and sorrow, whereas the one upon whom God shines, He gives him lasting joy, which is higher and sweeter than every earthly joy.

4.5.2.en: 2- This gladness in God's grace man receives through offering the sacrifices of prayer, worship and service, as we mentioned in (v. 5).

4.6.0.en: 8- I will both lay me down in peace, and sleep: for thou, Lord, only makest me dwell in safety.

4.6.1.en: 1- Since David's heart is filled with gladness and peace, because he trusted in God to whom he cried out and by whose light he was enlightened, he is able to lie down and sleep reassured in God's hands; as he began his day with crying out to God in (v. 1) in the midst of tribulations, he trusts that at the end of the day he can lie down and sleep in rest, because he is in God's care, and therefore this Psalm is said in the prayer of the Veil at the end of the day.

4.6.2.en: 2- Lying down and sleeping also apply to the repose of death; whoever lives with God a life of righteousness is in peace, so he does not fear death, but is alone and distinguished from other human beings in accepting death with reassurance in the hope of eternal life; thus in the Septuagint it says "Thou hast made me to dwell in hope."

4.6.3.en: 3- This verse is a prophecy about Christ, who lies down and sleeps in the tomb, alone among all mankind in that He will raise Himself on the third day.

4.6.4.en: 4- This verse gives peace to man, for everyone who sleeps alone, away from people, sleeps reassured, because he is in God's hands and in the hope that He will raise him to pray and live with Him. It applies to everyone who lives among many who do not feel for him and for all that he suffers, but God is with him, so even if he lies down and sleeps alone and solitary, he is reassured that he will awake and live with God.

4.6.5.en: If only you would pray deeply at the end of every day to be rid of all your cares and feel God, so that you sleep reassured in the hope that you will awake to praise Him and live for your sole aim, which is the love of God.

4.6.6.en: The blessings of the righteous and the judgment of the wicked To the chief Musician upon Nehiloth, A Psalm of David. "Give ear to my words, O Lord" ... (v. 1) Introduction:

4.6.7.en: 1- Its writer: the prophet David, as appears from the title of the Psalm.

4.6.8.en: 2- In this Psalm David implores God for the sake of sinners, and shows God's delight in His righteous children and His blessings for them. On the other hand, it shows His distress at the wicked and His punishing them.

4.6.9.en: 3- Some of the Fathers see that David wrote this Psalm out of distress over Ahithophel, who was David's counselor and then became counselor to his son Absalom, and gave counsel to kill David, so he is a traitor to his lord, whose service he enjoyed for many years. He is a type of Judas Iscariot, who betrayed Christ, and also a type of the Antichrist, who appears at the end of days and opposes Christ.

4.6.10.en: 4- This Psalm begins by speaking in the singular and ends by speaking in the plural, and this shows that everyone who prays has an individual relationship with God and at the same time is a member of the universal Church.

4.6.11.en: 5- In the title of this Psalm we find "to the chief Musician", that is, it was chanted by the leader of the singers with a large company, and this shows the importance of this Psalm.

4.6.12.en: 6- The title of this Psalm shows that it was chanted accompanied by wind musical instruments.

4.6.13.en: 7- This Psalm is considered a lament of David before the betrayal of Ahithophel, and it suits everyone who suffers betrayal by his loved ones. But the Psalm ends with hope and blessing for the one who lives with God; therefore it is fitting that man pray this Psalm in the morning, so that he is encouraged and not hindered by the wrongs of others against him.

4.6.14.en: 8- This Psalm is a morning prayer because it says "In the morning shalt thou hear my voice" ... (v. 3), that is, I rise early to You and pray; therefore the Church placed it in the prayer of Prime, so that man begins his day with it.

4.6.15.en: 9- It also suits the believer who goes to church in the morning and bows down before God's sanctuary and says "But as for me, I will come into thy house in the multitude of thy mercy" ... (v. 7).

5.0.0.en: 1- Give ear to my words, O Lord, consider my cry.

5.0.1.en: 1- Since David feels severe distress, he speaks with boldness to God, asking Him to give ear to the words of his prayers, and also to consider, that is, to understand his cry; giving ear means to hear with attention, and then he asks Him to feel for him and understand what he is suffering, while the cry means prayers from the heart. In another translation it says "my thought" instead of "my cry", that is, he asks God to understand his inner thoughts, so it is an inner cry and not an outward one, that is, a deep prayer, like Moses, who was praying when he reached the Red Sea and saw Pharaoh and his army attacking him, and God said to him, why do you cry to me; because the prayer of Moses was from his heart like a cry (Ex 14:15).

5.0.2.en: 2- David speaks with the boldness of a bride with her bridegroom, or a son with his father, so he does not beseech God to listen to him, but says directly, give ear, consider. He also speaks thus directly because he speaks as a father about his sinful children, and as a mother, who is the Church, about her children, so he speaks with boldness, that God may hear the prayers of all sinners who are in distress and have mercy on them.

5.1.0.en: 2- Hearken unto the voice of my cry, my King and my God: for unto thee will I pray.

5.1.1.en: 1- David also urges God to hear his prayer for himself and for his children, and for all who are tempted by betrayal or wrong from others.

5.1.2.en: 2- In these two verses he gives God three titles: the Lord, my King, and my God, and perhaps this points to the Holy Trinity. He also asks God three times to give ear, to suffer and to hear, and this too is a symbol of the Trinity, and points to the persistence and boldness in David's prayer.

5.1.3.en: 3- David asked God in his prayer for three things, which are:

5.1.4.en: a- Give ear, that is, listen with attention.

5.1.5.en: b- Consider; that is, understand after you have listened with attention.

5.1.6.en: c- Hearken; that is, do not neglect the words of prayer.

5.1.7.en: And that shows how much David needed God's intervention to support him and console him in his distress.

5.1.8.en: 4- And when David says to God "my King", this is a declaration from David that God is the true King over His people and David is His deputy, and thus every person who has a position of leadership should understand that God is the Head and King, while man is His deputy who must walk faithfully, to give his account to the true King.

5.2.0.en: 3- My voice shalt thou hear in the morning, O Lord; in the morning will I direct my prayer unto thee, and will look up.

5.2.1.en: In the morning: the early morning between dawn and sunrise.

5.2.2.en: 1- David declares that he offers this prayer in the early morning, and the morning means that he begins with God before any other work and relies on Him before seeking the help of any human being.

5.2.3.en: 2- The morning means activity, that is, man offers his best times to God, as the Scripture says, "those that seek me early shall find me" (Prov 8:17).

5.2.4.en: 3- The morning also means spiritual enlightenment, as the Sun of Righteousness, that is, Christ, rises upon him, so he prophesies about Christ who comes with His wondrous light after the darkness of the night, which signifies sin and weakness; if man has fallen into sins during the night of his life, he awakes from his heedlessness and stands for prayer.

5.2.5.en: 4- The morning means victory, because in it the resurrection of the Lord took place, who rose victorious and binding Satan. And in the morning the children of Israel looked and found the bodies of the Egyptians on the seashore, and they praised God (Ex 15). And in the morning the children of Israel, in the days of King Hezekiah, saw the bodies of the Assyrians of the army of Sennacherib, whom the angel had killed (2 Kgs 19:35).

5.2.6.en: 5- And in the morning Christians offer their sacrifice, that is, the sacrifice of the Eucharist, in the Liturgies, which are the greatest of prayers.

5.2.7.en: 6- David's faith appears in his waiting for God's answer when he directed his prayer toward Him, for he did not ask anyone else, because he trusts that God hears him and answers him. Perhaps by the spirit of prophecy he is speaking to us about Christ, whom he awaits to save mankind.

5.2.8.en: 7- Here David makes clear that prayer is not only speech from one side, which is man toward God, but is also a dialogue, as man hears God's voice and His answer, whether through feelings within his heart, or verses that come to his mind, or in any other way; the one who prays ought to wait to hear the voice of God, and it is not right to leave without waiting for God's reply. This requires faith so that man may experience deep, true prayer.

5.2.9.en: God rejoices in your prayer when you offer it from all your heart, understanding what you utter, whether in the prayers of the Agpeya or your own spontaneous prayers, and be confident that He hears you and answers you, but at the right time for the salvation of your soul.

5.3.s.en: (2) G does not take pleasure in evil

5.3.0.en: 4- For thou art not a God that hath pleasure in wickedness: neither shall evil dwell with thee.

5.3.1.en: 1- God did not create evil, but only good, and evil is the opposite of good, that is, when man separates himself from God, as Satan did, he becomes wicked, and does the opposite of God's commandments, just as night is the opposite of light; night is not something in itself, but merely the opposite of light, that is, when there is no light it is called night; so also evil is the opposite of good, and God is light and in Him is no darkness, and consequently He rejects evil. I cannot draw near to God while I keep evil within me, but I must hasten to repentance, that God may cleanse me.

5.3.2.en: 2- The wicked man cannot draw near to God, since God does not accept him, and he too fears to approach Him, since he is going in another direction than the light.

5.3.3.en: 3- The wicked man does not dwell with God, that is, he has no place in His Church, because he persists in evil. Therefore Paul commanded that the sinner of Corinth be set apart from the Church and put away (1 Cor 5:5).

5.3.4.en: 4- It is understood, of course, that the wicked man has no place in eternity, for he does not dwell with God forever.

5.3.5.en: 5- And if the wicked man does not dwell with God, then of course His children such as David cannot dwell with the wicked or mix with them in the close mixing that blends them together and influences them.

5.3.6.en: 6- If the wicked are enemies of God, then I am not troubled if one of them wrongs me, for he is hostile to God; so I am reassured that God will defend me, and I continue to love him and ask Him to lift his evil from me, and if He wishes to discipline him that he may repent, let it be God's will.

5.3.7.en: When you commit sin, know that you have rejected God, and God has also rejected you; therefore hasten to repentance, so that you do not lose your place in His embrace and can also enjoy His care.

5.4.0.en: 5- The boasters shall not stand in thy sight: thou hatest all workers of iniquity.

5.4.1.en: 1- In this verse he adds a focus on a great sin, which is the root of many sins, namely pride; the proud person, or the one who boasts in himself, cannot draw near or stand before God. He also affirms God's hatred of the one who does evil, and he means God's hatred of evil, but He wants all the wicked to return to Him by repentance, so He accepts them and forgives them.

5.4.2.en: 2- Pride blinds man's eyes to God and darkens his mind, so he thinks that what he does is right, and this makes him slip into many sins, and God hates all these sins; the tax collector received God's mercy by his humility and repentance, while the proud Pharisee added the sin of pride to his sins (Lk 18:10-14).

5.5.0.en: 6- Thou shalt destroy them that speak leasing: the Lord will abhor the bloody and deceitful man.

5.5.1.en: In this verse he focuses on other sins after pride, which are:

5.5.2.en: 1- Lying and deceit, which represent crookedness and deceiving others; whoever dares to deceive the image of God, that is, human beings, deceives God Himself, and he must perish.

5.5.3.en: 2- The unjust and cruel, that is, the bloody man, is the one who wrongs the innocent, and this one too must perish, because murder is a terrible sin; therefore the Jews deserved destruction, because they killed the prophets who proclaimed the name of the Lord, and then killed Christ Himself, who came to redeem them.

5.5.4.en: 3- This verse applies to Ahithophel, who plotted to kill his lord the king, and it also applies to Judas Iscariot the traitor, who delivered his Lord for the Jews to kill Him.

5.5.5.en: Whoever walks in evil against others not only makes enemies of them and of God, but is also an enemy to himself, because he condemns himself to destruction. It is spiritual blindness, which makes man not understand the gravity of the evil he is doing.

5.6.0.en: 7- But as for me, I will come into thy house in the multitude of thy mercy: and in thy fear will I worship in thy holy temple.

5.6.1.en: 1- Although the wicked do not dwell with God, David, who believes in God, declares the conduct of the righteous, which is to draw near to the house of God, that is, the Church, which was symbolized by the Ark of the Covenant in ancient times, and then by the temple of Solomon. There David and every believer declare their submission by bowing down before God in reverence and fear, rejecting all evil from the heart, declaring their repentance before the holy God.

5.6.2.en: 2- David declares that man is unworthy to enter the house of God, but it is God's mercy that allows man this great honor, because the house of God is the icon of heaven.

5.6.3.en: 3- Bowing down means man's lowliness because of his sins, as he brings his head to the ground, but in confidence in God's mercies he rises from the prostration, that is, the metanoia, and stands before God in hope and with the boldness of sonship, as St. Basil the Great says.

5.6.4.en: 4- Although David was driven out from before his son Absalom outside Jerusalem, in faith he is confident that he will return by God's mercy and enter His house and bow down before Him, as the prophet Jonah believed after him, while in the belly of the whale, that he would return and look upon God's temple (Jon 2:4).

5.6.5.en: 5- Because of the greatness of this verse the Church arranged that every deacon and every worshiper who enters the church should say it, bowing down before the sanctuary and saying this verse, and many churches have even written this verse above their sanctuaries.

5.7.0.en: 8- Lead me, O Lord, in thy righteousness because of mine enemies; make thy way straight before my face.

5.7.1.en: 1- As David enters the house of the Lord and bows down, he feels his need for a life of righteousness, and he has no way to it except God Himself; indeed, he attaches righteousness to God, saying "thy righteousness", and distinguishes it from the righteousness of the world, that is, all that the world thinks to be good morals and right conduct, because God's righteousness is higher than all this, for it springs from man's entering into God's embrace, so he puts on God and is united with Him, and God leads him accordingly in the way of righteousness.

5.7.2.en: 2- God's righteousness is being with Him, and consequently it is the Kingdom on earth; therefore we say in the Divine Liturgy "Guide us, O Lord, to Your Kingdom."

5.7.3.en: 3- The wicked try to hinder David and every believer from the life of righteousness; therefore David asks God to remove the obstacles that the wicked placed in the way of righteousness, so that He makes his way toward God easy. Our enemies are the demons, who try to hinder us with evil lusts, preoccupations and problems, but they have no authority over us, because God is able to make our way to Him easy.

5.7.4.en: 4- This verse shows David's longings for a life of perfection and the completion of his worship, so he asks for a way toward God in which He guides him, that he may reach the righteousness of God and not be hindered by all the hindrances of Satan.

5.7.5.en: Set your goal before you, which is the life of righteousness, have a spiritual rule, and ask God's help to lead you and support you, so that you enter every day into new depths in fellowship with God and live the Kingdom while you are on earth.

5.8.s.en: (4) The judgment of G on the wicked

5.8.0.en: 9- For there is no truth in their mouths; their inward part is an abyss; their throat is an open sepulchre; they have polished their tongues. Polished: said of a sword or a knife, that is, making it sharp and smooth, and what is meant here is that the tongue is harmful.

5.8.1.en: Here the prophet David shows the gravity of the evil that his enemies do, and the enemies, as we said, are the demons and all who follow them in their conduct and slip into their evils, so he declares their gravity in the following:

5.8.2.en: a- "There is no truth in their mouths": that is, their speech is falsehood; they are deceivers, cheats, trying to lead God's children astray with hypocrisy, or wrong counsel, and with thoughts that seem good but contain the poison of death.

5.8.3.en: b- Their inward part is an abyss, that is, they are never satisfied with evil and injustice and wronging others, so they kill many with the arrows of their sins and swallow them up like a bottomless abyss. Consequently the demons cannot be appeased, but must be overcome by the power of God.

5.8.4.en: c- Their throat is an open sepulchre: the stench of death appears in their speech, like an open grave from which the foul smell rises. The meaning of this is that their speech harms God's children and leads them astray, like the heretics, or the proud and selfish, who harm those around them, and also the unjust, who suck the blood of the righteous, so they die, in order to achieve their personal interests.

5.8.5.en: d- They have polished their tongues, so their speech is sharp and painful to others, so they wrong God's children with insults and reproach, and also with hypocrisy and dissimulation, and they slaughter them as a sword wounds and slaughters and kills. And their tongues are polished, that is, trained in evil.

5.8.6.en: David shows the gravity of the wicked in order to ask great help from God, that He may protect him from them, and also to be careful to keep away from them, so that his heart is not influenced by their evils.

5.9.0.en: 10- Destroy thou them, O God; let them fall by their own counsels; cast them out in the multitude of their transgressions; for they have rebelled against thee.

5.9.1.en: 1- In this verse David states the natural result of evil, which is that God will judge the wicked and call them to account for all their sins.

5.9.2.en: 2- And when David says "Destroy thou them, O God" he does not mean personal vengeance for himself, but states a fact, which is the punishment of the wicked, perhaps this will alert the wicked, that they may repent.

5.9.3.en: 3- David also declares that the wicked will fall into God's just hand because of all their plots that they devised against God's children. The plots of the wicked turn back upon their own heads and destroy them, as happened in the plot of Haman against Mordecai, for instead of Mordecai being hanged, the king hanged Haman on the same gallows that Haman had prepared for Mordecai (Esth 7:10).

5.9.4.en: 4- Because of the multitude of the transgressions of the wicked, God will punish them by casting them into the abyss, that is, eternal torment, for every idle word man will give account of it in the day of judgment, how much more all his evil deeds.

5.9.5.en: 5- Here David affirms that the evils of the wicked are rebellion against God, and not merely a wrong to a weak human being like David, and consequently the wicked await God's justice and His punishment.

5.9.6.en: Remember the punishment of sin, so that you keep away, not only from evil, but from everything that leads to it. And so long as you are striving on the way of repentance, be confident that God supports you and delivers you, however weak you are.

5.10.s.en: (5) The blessings of G for the righteous

5.10.0.en: 11- But let all that put their trust in thee rejoice; they shall ever shout for joy, and thou shalt overshadow them; and they that love thy name shall be joyful in thee.

5.10.1.en: 1- At the end of the Psalm David declares God's blessings for His children, and they are the opposite of the punishment of the wicked mentioned in the previous verse. God's children rejoice on earth in His care for them, and this is a pledge of their lasting joy in the Kingdom of Heaven. This joy is enjoyed only by everyone who trusted in God and not in himself or the powers of the world.

5.10.2.en: 2- From the joy of God's children they shout, that is, they glorify God and proclaim His name before those around them; indeed, their joy in itself is the glorification of God in the midst of a world depressed because of sin.

5.10.3.en: 3- The shouting is also the hymns of thanksgiving to God, which the Church lifts up every day and continues in forever, since the only work of God's children in the Kingdom is praise.

5.10.4.en: 4- God's children also enjoy that God overshadows them, that is, He cares for them with His love and satisfies them with His presence with them. This too begins on earth, when they feel God's embrace and the warmth of His love, and then they discover new depths of His love in heaven.

5.10.5.en: 5- Everyone who loved the name of God and trusted in Him and praised Him and lived for Him as his only goal is, of course, the one who will be glad and rejoice with Him forever.

5.10.6.en: 6- For the sake of these joys and glories the Septuagint puts as a title for this Psalm "Unto the end, for her that inherits", that is, God's work in His children is completed unto the end, that is, forever in the Kingdom, and there He gives them their eternal inheritance.

5.10.7.en: 7- We note in this verse that he speaks about the believers as a community, that is, the Church, and not as an individual, as he began his supplications at the beginning of the Psalm about himself and as an intercessor for his people, so he concludes the Psalm with the joy of God's children on earth and in heaven.

5.11.0.en: 12- For thou, Lord, wilt bless the righteous; with favour wilt thou compass him as with a shield. Shield: a piece of wood having a handle at the back in which the soldier puts his hand and moves this wood before his head and body, to protect himself from the arrows of the enemy.

5.11.1.en: 1- In conclusion God declares His blessing to His children who hold fast to Him, and this blessing satisfies and suffices His children, so they need nothing from the world and are not troubled or disturbed over any gain or loss.

5.11.2.en: 2- God surrounds His children and protects them, as the soldier protects himself with the shield; indeed, God is distinguished in His protection in that He is a shield on all sides, that is, complete protection. This shield results from God's favor toward them. And this shield is God's fatherhood and His love, which protect His children, so no one can harm them. And even if they walk in the midst of tribulations, God keeps their inner peace for them.

5.11.3.en: 3- This shield, with which God surrounds His children, is also like a crown on their heads, which gladdens their hearts, as the Septuagint says, "Thou hast crowned us as with a shield of good pleasure."

5.11.4.en: 4- And the shield, as Paul the Apostle says, is "the shield of faith" (Eph 6:16); everyone who believes in God and relies on Him, God surrounds him with His care.

5.11.5.en: If only you would look to the eternal recompense, so that your heart does not cling to the enticements of the world, but you bear tribulations and ask the help of God, who protects you and brings you to His Kingdom.

5.11.6.en: The acceptance of the cry of a penitent To the chief Musician on Neginoth upon Sheminith, A Psalm of David. "O Lord, rebuke me not in thine anger, neither chasten me in thy hot displeasure" ... (v. 1) Introduction:

5.11.7.en: 1- Its writer: the prophet David, who lived the feelings of repentance in their deepest form.

5.11.8.en: 2- This Psalm is the first of the seven penitential Psalms, which are (6, 32, 38, 51, 102, 130, 143) as determined by St. Augustine.

5.11.9.en: 3- It was prayed every day in the synagogues of the Jews, and is now prayed in the prayer of Prime in the Agpeya in the Coptic Orthodox Church, and is also prayed in the Latin Church.

5.11.10.en: 4- The title of the Psalm shows that it was repeated by the chief Musician, that is, it is a Psalm for the people that the people repeat, and this is what happens in the Old and New Testaments, as we mentioned.

5.11.11.en: 5- This Psalm was accompanied by a stringed musical instrument called Neginoth, which has eight strings; for the title of this Psalm in the Septuagint is Octave, that is, eight in the Latin language. Perhaps eight signifies the day of judgment, when God accepts the penitent and glorifies them with Him, especially as the Septuagint puts as a title for this Psalm "Unto the end", that is, unto the day of judgment.

5.11.12.en: 6- At the end of the title of the Psalm it says "upon Sheminith", and the Sheminith is a degree among the registers of the voice.
